source.title: Do Flatter Minima Drive Better Generalization? An Algorithmic Separation in Grokking

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including the appendix; no apparent truncation or garbling affects the reported findings.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own results arguing that flatter solutions do not reliably select generalizing solutions in grokking, while SAM can speed a transition when weight decay is present. It does not test the specific claim versions’ named settings or measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper tests SAM and weight decay on grokking tasks, measures sharpness and generalization transitions, and analyzes a constructed interpolating network. The cited studies and results are not extracted as this study’s results. Parameter values and curvature metrics are not rows solely because they are used to choose or characterize a condition.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether SAM-induced flatness selects or accelerates generalization in grokking. None of V1–V8 names that claim. In particular, V7 concerns the correlation and ranking performance of magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, not whether Hessian flatness causally induces generalization. The study's Hessian, normalized-Hessian and final-layer relative-flatness measures do not test V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors argue that SAM-induced flatness alone does not reliably select generalization in modular-arithmetic grokking, whereas weight decay favors generalizing solutions and SAM can accelerate their emergence. They also explicitly claim flatness is unnecessary. That stronger claim concerns their flatness measures and studied regimes; it is not a test of V7's correlational magnitude-aware sharpness claim. The practical-task results establish epoch-level acceleration rather than isolating the same causal mechanism.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines grokking with SAM and weight decay, plus a theoretical two-layer ReLU construction; it does not reproduce the claim versions’ specified experiments or measures.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported acceleration varies with SAM radius ρ: it generally rises as ρ increases, then can decline once the first-order Taylor estimate becomes inaccurate. The study also reports different speedups across task and Transformer depth; one 2-layer add-mod-97 condition is slower than the weight-decay baseline.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM-only modular-arithmetic runs fail to grok despite flatter final solutions; WD-based runs reach the transition in 198/200 cases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested modular-arithmetic settings, low Hessian sharpness does not suffice to select generalizing solutions.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM+WD usually reaches the generalization transition in fewer epochs, reaching 3.992x acceleration in one condition, with a 0.903x slowdown in another.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM can accelerate grokking when combined with weight decay, depending on radius, task and architecture; epoch savings do not establish compute savings.

fits_no_version.finding: Constructed memorizing and generalizing interpolants have equal Hessian trace, while the generalizing construction has lower norm for sufficiently large training sets; the quadratic SAM analysis gives a conditional instability window.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this construction, Hessian trace does not distinguish generalization, whereas parameter norm and optimizer-dependent stability can separate aspects of the solutions.

record.problems: The paper states that the theoretical analysis uses an analytically tractable setup and quadratic SAM approximation, and does not establish unchanged thresholds for cross-entropy, attention, normalization, or minibatch training. For vision and language tasks it says it cannot isolate the causal mechanisms as readily. Speedup is epoch-level and does not account for SAM’s additional computational cost. Practical-task speedup values are shown in figures without numeric values in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No separate row was created for every modular task × architecture × ρ combination or each listed curvature metric in Tables 2–3; the key transition counts and speedup variation are summarized in R1–R7. Figure-only practical-task speedups are represented as qualitative results in R8–R10 because the supplied text gives no exact plotted values.

untested.parts: Matched random-label and natural-label fitting and held-out accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under specified tuning budgets and recovery recipes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its correlation with generalization gaps, and its ranking relative to norm- and margin-based measures among comparable convolutional networks.
Accuracy after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because no row measures a version; this does not negate their reported grokking findings. No original-source exclusion applies. The supplied text was sufficient for this assessment.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label fitting or natural-label comparison.
No width sweep past an interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD or momentum SGD.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets.

The study measures Hessian and relative-flatness metrics and analyzes trace flatness, but does not test the version’s magnitude-aware perturbation measure or its comparison across a convolutional family at similarly low training loss.

rows.operation_detail: Posthoc measurement of final-checkpoint training-loss Hessian maximum eigenvalue.

rows.baseline: No-regularization and weight-decay-based runs are reported as sharper comparators
rows.value: SAM-only finds by far the flattest solutions; no run generalizes

rows.subject: Two-layer ReLU interpolating network
rows.operation_detail: Analytically compares trace flatness of constructed memorizing and generalizing interpolants at the same scale.
rows.note: The paper’s construction states that flatness does not separate the two interpolants.
rows.check: Equality of Hessian traces in constructed ReLU interpolants does not test V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure or its empirical ranking claim.

rows.subject: Two-layer ReLU interpolating network
rows.operation_detail: Analytically compares parameter norms of constructed memorizing and generalizing interpolants.

conditions.value: sufficiently large n, with theorem threshold n > 2C (r²(C+(C−1)²)+r⁻²)/(r²(d+(d−1)²)+r⁻²)

rows.note: The authors interpret lower norm as favoring the generalizing branch under weight decay.
rows.check: Parameter-norm separation does not measure any version. Correct the threshold's leading factor to 2^C, the number of generalizing neurons, rather than 2C.

rows.subject: Two-layer ReLU interpolating network
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes local linear stability of a memorizing interpolant under gradient descent and the quadratic SAM approximation.

conditions.value: r ∈ (rlow, rhigh), described as a low-norm window

rows.note: The theorem says this window exists subject to its stated thresholds and quadratic SAM approximation.
rows.check: Optimizer-dependent local stability does not measure any version. Describe the proof as a top/nonzero-curvature-mode comparison under quadratic SAM, conditional on a nonempty threshold window. Its strict full-space stability definition is problematic because zero Hessian modes have update multiplier one.
